figures.caption: Table 1: Main benchmark results. (a) Comparison with 7B-class large VLAs on LIBERO (success rate %); Mind-VLA matches them with a backbone 9–20× smaller. (b) Comparison on CALVIN ABC-D (average completed length over 1000 rollouts; †Large VLA). Best results are bolded.
Figure 3: Mind-VLA vs. compact-backbone baselines on LIBERO. Per-suite success rate (%). Bold-italic labels mark Mind-VLA’s value; lighter italic labels mark the best non-Mind-VLA baseline per suite.

Figure 1: Comparison of 3D-aware VLA paradigms. Existing 3D-aware VLA methods are fundamentally instruction-agnostic. They either provide instruction-agnostic 3D features as additional model inputs (a) [6, 5, 7] or align VLA representations with instruction-agnostic 3D features during training (b) [8, 9], neglecting the 3D geometry of the specific target object designated by the language instruction. (c) Mind-VLA (Ours) aligns VLA representations with instruction-aware 3D features during training, enabling instruction-aware 3D understanding.

Table 2: Ablation on LIBERO. Top: progressive build-up of auxiliary components (A0–A2). Bottom: scene-image (instruction-agnostic) vs. target-object tri-view (ours) VGGT alignment, both added on top of A2. Success rate (%); best results in each column bolded.

Figure 4: Real robot setup and tasks. (a) Dual-arm xArm 6 workspace (one arm used) with static and wrist-mounted cameras. (b) Example tasks under normal conditions: Pick, Place, and Drawer. (c) Occluded conditions for Pick and Drawer, where ∼25% of the target is blocked by a physical occluder (highlighted in red).

Figure 2: Overview of Mind-VLA. Instructions, states, and observations are tokenized and processed by a transformer backbone together with three groups of learnable queries. Scene queries are decoded into per-patch RGB and dense 2D motion. Object queries are decoded into a target-object tri-view latent. The backbone is also aligned with VGGT [27] features extracted from the same triview at four intermediate layers. Action queries condition a diffusion transformer [32] that predicts the next three actions. The right panel shows the attention mask, which enforces temporal causality and separates different query groups. Auxiliary branches are used only during training.
Table 3: Real-robot per-task success rate (%); 30 trials per cell.
